passages.source_text: ταῦτα τοῦ Ἀππίωνος ἀλληγοροῦντος, σύννους ὢν ἐγὼ ἔδοξα τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένοις μὴ παρακολουθεῖν, διὸ τὸν λόγον ἐγκόψας ἔφη μοι Εἰ μὴ παρακολουθεῖς οἷς λέγω, τί καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν διαλέγομαι; κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Μή με ὑπολάμβανε ἀναισθήτως ἔχειν τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ λεγομένων· πάνυ γὰρ αὐτὰ συνίημι, ἅτε δὴ οὐ πρῶτον αὐτῶν ἀκηκοώς. ἵνα δὲ γνῷς ὅτι οὐκ ἀγνοῶ τὰ ὑπὸ σοῦ λεγόμενα, τὰ μὲν σοι ῥηθέντα ἐπιτεμοῦμαι, τῶν δὲ παραλειφθέντων σοι κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν ὡς παρ’ ἑτέρων ἤκουσα, ἀποπληρώσω τὰς ἀλληγορίας. καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἔφη Ποίησον οὕτως ὡς λέγεις.

κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Παρίημι νῦν ἐπ’ ἀκριβὲς λέγειν τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀπείρου ὕλης κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν κράσεως ἀποκυηθὲν ἔμψυχον ὠόν, οὗ ῥαγέντος κατὰ τινὰς ἀρρενόθηλυ ἐξέθορεν, Φάνης. καὶ πάντ’ ἐκεῖνα ἐπιτέμνομαι, μέχρις οὗ τὸ ῥαγὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν, ὑπολειφθείσης αὐτοῦ μυελώδους ὕλης, καὶ τὸν λόγον τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἔνδοθεν γενομένων ἐπὶ κεφαλαίων μετὰ τῶν ἀκολούθων ἐπιτρέχω. ἐγεννήθη γὰρ (ὡς λέγεις) ἐκ Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας (ὑπό τε χρόνου καὶ ὕλης) τὰ μὲν πρῶτα Πλούτων, ὡς ἡ κάτω παραχωρήσασα ὑποστάθμη — δεύτερα δὲ Ποσειδῶν, ὃς ἡ μέση ἐστὶν ὑγρὰ οὐσία ἐπιπολάσασα τῇ κάτω ὀλκοτάτῃ φύσει — ἡ δὲ τρίτη ἀνωτάτη τε καὶ αἰθὴρ οὖσα, ὅσπερ ἐστὶν Ζεύς, ἥτις οὐ κατεπόθη, ἀλλὰ θερμὴ οὖσα ἰσχὺς καὶ ἀνωφερῆ ἔχουσα τὴν φύσιν ὥσπερ ὑπὸ τινὸς ῥιπῆς εἰς τὸν ἄνω ἡγεμονικώτατον ἀνέπτη αἰθέρα.

δεσμὰ δὲ τὰ Κρόνου ἐστὶν ἡ σύμπηξις οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὡς καὶ ἄλλων ἀλληγορούντων ἀκήκοα, ἡ δὲ ἀποκοπὴ τῶν μορίων ὁ τῶν στοιχείων χωρισμὸς καὶ διάκρισις, ὅτι πάντα ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀπετμήθη καὶ ἀφωρίσθη καθ’ ἑαυτὰ τετάχθαι ἕκαστον· καὶ οὐκέτι γεννᾷ χρόνος, ἀλλὰ τὰ γεννηθέντα δι’ αὐτοῦ νόμῳ φύσεως ποιεῖται τὰς διαδοχάς. ἡ δὲ ἐκ τοῦ βυθοῦ ἀνακύψασα Ἀφροδίτη ἡ ἐκ τοῦ ὑγροῦ γόνιμος οὐσία, ᾗ τὸ θερμὸν πνεῦμα μιγὲν τὸν τῆς μίξεως ποιεῖται ἔρωτα καὶ τελεσιουργεῖ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ κάλλος.

τὸ δὲ συμπόσιον τὸ γαμήλιον, ἔνθα τὸ δεῖπνον ἐτέλει Ζεὺς ὑπέρ τε τῆς Νηρηΐδος Θέτιδος καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ Πηλέως, ἀλληγορίαν ἔχει ταύτην, ἵνα γνῷς ὅτι καὶ ἄνευ σου, Ἀππίων, τὰ τοιαῦτα ἠκούσαμεν. τὸ μὲν δὴ συμπόσιον ὁ κόσμος, οἱ δὲ δώδεκα τὰ οὐράνια τῶν Μοιρῶν περιστηρίγματα, ἅτινα ζῴδια καλοῦσιν — Προμηθεὺς ἡ προμήθεια, ὑφ’ ἧς τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο — Πηλεὺς πηλὸς ὁ ἀπὸ γῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν περινοηθεὶς καὶ μιγεὶς τῇ Νηρηΐδι, τουτέστιν ὕδατι. ἐκ δὲ τῆς τῶν δύο μίξεως (ὕδατός τε καὶ γῆς) ὁ πρῶτος οὐ γεννηθεὶς ἀλλὰ πλασθεὶς τέλειος καὶ διὰ τὸ μαζοῖς χείλη μὴ προσενεγκεῖν Ἀχιλλεὺς προσηγορεύθη· ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμήν, ἥτις ἐὰν ἐπιθυμίαν (Πολυξένην) ὡς ἀληθείας ἀλλοτρίαν οὖσαν καὶ ξένην ἐπιθυμῇ, ἰῷ ὄφεως ἀναιρεῖται βέλει κατὰ πτέρναν καὶ κατὰ ἴχνος ἐνέρποντος τοῦ θανάτου.

Ἥρα τοίνυν καὶ Ἀθηνᾶ καὶ Ἀφροδίτη καὶ Ἔρις καὶ μῆλον καὶ Ἑρμῆς καὶ κρίσις καὶ ποιμὴν τοιοῦτόν τινα νοῦν ὑπαινίσσεται· Ἥρα σεμνότης, Ἀθηνᾶ ἡ ἀνδρεία, Ἀφροδίτη αἱ ἡδοναί, Ἑρμῆς ὁ ἑρμηνευτικὸς λόγος, ὁ ποιμὴν Πάρις ἡ ἀλόγιστος ὁρμὴ καὶ βάρβαρος. ἐὰν οὖν κατὰ τὴν ἀκμὴν τῆς ἡλικίας ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν ποιμαίνων λογισμὸς τύχῃ ὢν βάρβαρος καὶ παραλιπὼν τὰ συμφέροντα (ἀνδρείαν τέ καὶ σωφροσύνην παρωσάμενος) μόνας ἕληται τὰς ἡδονὰς καὶ μόνῃ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τὴν νίκην ἀποδῷ, ὡς παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ τέρποντα ἀντιλαμβάνων: ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ ὁ μὴ ὀρθῶς κρίνας τὴν τέρψιν λήμψεται. Ἔρις δὲ ἐστὶν ἡ φιλονεικοῦσα κακία. τὸ δὲ τῶν Ἑσπερίδων χρυσοῦν μῆλον ὁ πλοῦτος ἂν εἴη, ὃς ἐνίοτε καὶ τοὺς σώφρονας (ὥσπερ τὴν Ἥραν) πρὸς ῥαθυμίαν παράγειν ἐπίσταται καὶ τοὺς ἀνδρείους (ὥσπερ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν) εἰς τὰ μὴ αὐτοῖς πρέποντα φιλονεικοτέρους ἀπεργάζεται καὶ ψυχῆς κάλλος (ὥσπερ Ἀφροδίτην) , προφάσει τρυφῆς ἀπολλύει. συντόμως ἐρῶ· πάντας εἰς κακὴν ἔριν ἀνερεθίζει ὁ πλοῦτος.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: While Appion was interpreting these things allegorically, I was deep in thought and appeared not to be following what he was saying. So he broke off his discourse and said to me, “If you are not following what I am saying, why am I even having this discussion in the first place?” I replied, “Do not suppose that I am insensible to what you are saying, for I understand it very well, since this is not the first time I have heard it. To let you know that I am not ignorant of what you are saying, I will summarize what you have stated; and as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence, just as I heard them from others.” Appion said, “Do as you say.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σύννους ὢν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I was deep in thought
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύννους describes being absorbed or pensive, which explains why Clement merely appeared not to be following.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένοις μὴ παρακολουθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to be following what he was saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρακολουθέω here denotes following or comprehending the course of an argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ μὲν σοι ῥηθέντα ἐπιτεμοῦμαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will summarize what you have stated
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτέμνομαι means to abridge or summarize; the dative σοι is understood as identifying the person by whom the preceding statements were made.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν δὲ παραλειφθέντων σοι κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν is taken as describing an orderly continuation; “by logical consequence” is also possible.

passages.text: And I replied, “I now pass over giving a detailed account of the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter. When it burst, according to some, a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out. I also summarize all those matters up to the point when the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure, while marrow-like matter from it remained; then, in outline, I run through the account of the things produced inwardly by that matter, together with what follows. For, as you say, from Cronus and Rhea—that is, by time and matter—were born first Pluto, as the sediment that settled below; second Poseidon, who is the middle, moist substance floating above the nature with the strongest downward pull; and third the highest substance, which is aether, namely Zeus. This third substance was not swallowed, but, being a hot force and having a nature that rises upward, it flew up, as if driven by some gust, into the most sovereign aether above.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: And I replied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrative introduction explicitly identifies the following account as Clement’s reply and is retained before the direct speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀπείρου ὕλης κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν κράσεως ἀποκυηθὲν ἔμψυχον ὠόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔμψυχον is rendered “living” rather than the more technical “ensouled”; κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν presents the blending as occurring by chance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀρρενόθηλυ ἐξέθορεν, Φάνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter compound ἀρρενόθηλυ denotes an androgynous or male-and-female entity, while ἐξέθορεν conveys a sudden springing forth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ῥαγὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύτος can denote a hollow vessel, casing, or shell; τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν indicates acquiring an ordered or harmonious arrangement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ κάτω παραχωρήσασα ὑποστάθμη
lexical_decisions.chosen: the sediment that settled below
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment or dregs, and παραχωρήσασα depicts it giving way or moving to the lower position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ κάτω ὀλκοτάτῃ φύσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: the nature with the strongest downward pull
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual ὀλκοτάτῃ is understood from the idea of drawing or pulling, while κάτω specifies a downward tendency. “The lowest, most attractive nature” is a possible alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἄνω ἡγεμονικώτατον ἀνέπτη αἰθέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: it flew up into the most sovereign aether above
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἡγεμονικώτατον characterizes the upper aether as ruling or preeminent; “most ruling” would be less idiomatic English.

passages.text: Cronus’s bonds are the fastening together of heaven and earth, as I have also heard from others who give allegorical interpretations. The cutting off of his parts is the separation and differentiation of the elements, because all things were cut away from their own natural substance and set apart, each to be arranged by itself. Time no longer begets; instead, the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law. Aphrodite, who rose from the depth, is the generative substance arising from moisture. When the hot spirit mingles with it, it produces the desire for their union and brings the beauty of the world to completion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ σύμπηξις οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the fastening together of heaven and earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύμπηξις denotes a joining, compacting, or solid fastening together.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ἀποκοπὴ τῶν μορίων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the cutting off of his parts
lexical_decisions.rationale: μορίων is the source’s euphemistic “parts”; the possessive “his” refers contextually to Cronus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀπετμήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: all things were cut away from their own natural substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ is retained as marking source or separation. “Were divided according to their respective natures” is contextually possible but renders ἐκ less directly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ γεννηθέντα δι’ αὐτοῦ νόμῳ φύσεως ποιεῖται τὰς διαδοχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb; διαδοχάς may denote successive generations or succession more generally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τῆς μίξεως ποιεῖται ἔρωτα
lexical_decisions.chosen: it produces the desire for their union
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως can mean desire or erotic impulse, while τῆς μίξεως may describe either desire for the mixture or desire generated by it; the former fits the generative context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τελεσιουργεῖ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ κάλλος
lexical_decisions.chosen: brings the beauty of the world to completion
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελεσιουργέω means to accomplish, perfect, or bring something fully into effect.

passages.text: The wedding banquet, where Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus, has the following allegory—so that you may know, Appion, that we have heard such things even without you. The banquet, then, is the world; the twelve are the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports, which they call zodiacal signs; Prometheus is forethought, through which all things came to be; Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being and mixed with the Nereid—that is, with water. From the mixture of the two, water and earth, the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete; because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles. He himself also represents the prime of life. If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth, it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δεῖπνον ἐτέλει Ζεὺς ὑπέρ τε τῆς Νηρηΐδος Θέτιδος καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ Πηλέως
lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελεῖν a feast means to conduct or celebrate it; ὑπέρ identifies those for whom or in whose honor it is held.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ οὐράνια τῶν Μοιρῶν περιστηρίγματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιστηρίγματα is rare and denotes structures set or supporting something around a circumference; “surrounding fixtures” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Προμηθεὺς ἡ προμήθεια
lexical_decisions.chosen: Prometheus is forethought
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the explicit etymological wordplay between Προμηθεύς and προμήθεια.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Πηλεὺς πηλὸς ὁ ἀπὸ γῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν περινοηθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: πηλός preserves the wordplay with Peleus. περινοηθείς is taken in its mental sense, “conceived” or “devised,” though “selected” is also contextually possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πρῶτος οὐ γεννηθεὶς ἀλλὰ πλασθεὶς τέλειος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine ὁ πρῶτος resumes the preceding ἀνθρώπου. τέλειος can mean complete, perfect, mature, or full-grown.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ μαζοῖς χείλη μὴ προσενεγκεῖν Ἀχιλλεὺς προσηγορεύθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source supplies an allegorical etymology linking Achilles with the absence of nursing at the breast; the explanation is preserved without replacing it with a modern etymology.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥτις ἐὰν ἐπιθυμίαν (Πολυξένην) ὡς ἀληθείας ἀλλοτρίαν οὖσαν καὶ ξένην ἐπιθυμῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ὡς with οὖσαν descriptively, characterizing Desire as alien and foreign to truth. More explicitly it could be rendered “desires Desire as being alien and foreign to truth”; ὡς with the participle can also present this characterization as the represented reason or ground, yielding a causal sense such as “because she is alien and foreign to truth.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἰῷ ὄφεως ἀναιρεῖται βέλει κατὰ πτέρναν καὶ κατὰ ἴχνος ἐνέρποντος τοῦ θανάτου
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads both ἰῷ and βέλει instrumentally, attaches κατὰ πτέρναν to the arrow, and takes ἴχνος as a footprint or track with death’s creeping entrance. The instruments may instead be appositional or describe venom conveyed by the arrow. Moreover, ἴχνος can mean the sole or foot, and both coordinated κατὰ phrases may go with death’s entrance: “with death creeping in at the heel and at the sole of the foot.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμήν, ἥτις
source_issues.issue: The printed ἀκμήν is formally accusative or adverbial, whereas a predicate after ἔστι and the feminine nominative relative ἥτις would ordinarily call for ἀκμή. The context supports reference to the prime of life, but that interpretation remains provisional and is disclosed rather than treated as though the supplied Greek already contained the nominative form.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμή, ἥτις

passages.text: Hera, then, and Athena and Aphrodite and Eris and the apple and Hermes and the judgment and the shepherd hint at some such meaning: Hera is dignity; Athena, courage; Aphrodite, pleasures; Hermes, interpreting reason; and Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse. So if, at the prime of life, the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul happens to be barbarous and, passing over what is beneficial—thrusting aside both courage and self-control—chooses pleasures alone and awards victory to desire alone, as though receiving delightful things from her in return, then the one who judged wrongly will receive enjoyment to the destruction of both himself and all that is his. Eris is contentious vice. The golden apple of the Hesperides would be wealth, which sometimes knows how to lead even the self-controlled—as Hera—toward idleness, makes the courageous—as Athena—more contentious over things unfitting for them, and, under the pretext of luxury, destroys beauty of soul—as Aphrodite. I will put it briefly: wealth provokes everyone to evil strife.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἑρμῆς ὁ ἑρμηνευτικὸς λόγος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Hermes, interpreting reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here belongs to the psychological allegory and is therefore rendered “reason”; ἑρμηνευτικός also sustains the wordplay with Hermes. “Interpretive discourse” is possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ποιμὴν Πάρις ἡ ἀλόγιστος ὁρμὴ καὶ βάρβαρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁρμή denotes impulse or drive, while ἀλόγιστος marks it as lacking rational deliberation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν ποιμαίνων λογισμὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the shepherd image in ποιμαίνων and distinguishes λογισμός as the faculty of calculation or reasoning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ τέρποντα ἀντιλαμβάνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though receiving delightful things from her in return
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντιλαμβάνων expresses receiving something in exchange or return; ὡς allows the motivation to be presented as the reasoner’s supposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to the destruction of both himself and all that is his
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival τῶν αὐτοῦ is broad. In the Paris allegory it may refer to his people or household, but it can also denote his possessions; “all that is his” is intended to leave both personal and nonpersonal referents open.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ φιλονεικοῦσα κακία
lexical_decisions.chosen: contentious vice
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλονεικοῦσα characterizes vice as loving disputes or strife.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προφάσει τρυφῆς
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of luxury
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις is a pretext or professed ground, while τρυφή denotes luxury, indulgence, or soft living.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
